claims.text: Engineered short-range chemical ordering can be introduced at multilayer Al0.1CrCoFeNi coating interfaces.
Increasing interfacial SRO increases the activation energy for dislocation motion.
Increasing the activation energy for dislocation motion reduces creep in these coatings.
Al0.1CrCoFeNi multilayer coatings deposited under standard conditions have a predominantly random interfacial chemical distribution.
Changing substrate temperature and deposition rate can induce different degrees of interfacial SRO in Al0.1CrCoFeNi multilayers.
Atom probe tomography can quantify the proposed interfacial SRO.
Local chemical ordering at multilayer interfaces changes the spatial distribution of activation-energy barriers to dislocation glide.
Enhanced SRO creates a heterogeneous energy landscape.
The SRO-induced energy landscape elevates local barriers to dislocation motion and reduces dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation mobility diminishes time-dependent plastic deformation under sustained load.
Coatings with greater engineered SRO will have higher initial hardness than near-random controls.
Coatings with greater engineered SRO will exhibit enhanced strain hardening.
Coatings with greater engineered SRO will exhibit significantly less creep deformation than near-random controls.
Quantified SRO intensity will correlate directly with activation-energy barriers.
The proposed SRO effect applies from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures while the solid-state structure remains stable.
Phase transformations caused by extreme temperatures or prolonged exposure could invalidate the SRO-mediated creep resistance.
